### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, activity A13 was spread thinly across a wide pool of resources — 44 distinct resources in total, with the most frequent of them, User_10, handling only about 8 in 100 of its executions. In the later window, A13 was handled by User_10 alone: all 259 recorded executions in that window, with its concentration index rising from about 0.03 to 1. [ASSIGN002, CONC001]
- Activity A01 was reallocated as well. Earlier, its executions were led by User_10 (about 10 in 100) and User_49 (about 7 in 100), with roughly half spread thinly over many other resources; in the later window, User_10's share fell to about 6 in 100, User_49 and the other former leaders dropped out of the leading group, and a largely different set of resources, each taking roughly 4–7 in 100, took over. [ASSIGN001]
- Activity A22 shows the same kind of shift: earlier it was led by User_49 (about 12 in 100) and User_10 (about 8 in 100); in the later window User_49 no longer appears among the leading resources, User_10 fell to about 5 in 100, and a largely new set of resources took over, led by User_19 at about 9 in 100. [ASSIGN003]
- The resources that gained share at A01 and at A22 overlap heavily, as do those that lost share, so the three shifts look like one reallocation of work between two groups of resources rather than three unrelated changes. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN003]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that resource allocation changed for activities A01, A13 and A22: in the later window, executions of these three activities were assigned to a largely different set of resources, with A13 moving from a pool of about 44 resources to exclusive handling by User_10. This rests on direct allocation evidence: the resource family produced four qualifying items where about 0.01 would be expected by chance if nothing had changed, while no control-flow or timing item qualified; every item's difference is larger than in all but about 1 of 2,000 random re-splits of the pooled data; the two A13 items describe one and the same shift from complementary angles (assignment profile and concentration, on about 270 versus 260 executions), so they corroborate but do not independently confirm each other; and the A01 and A22 profiles rest on 200 and roughly 110 observations per window respectively. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, CONC001]

The evidence cannot show why the allocation changed, and because the resource codes are anonymous it cannot rule out that the pool of active resources itself changed composition (new codes replacing old ones) rather than assignment behaviour changing within a stable pool; for A01 and A22 the change is a broad redistribution across many resources, so no single reassignment can be pinpointed. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, CONC001]

Other differences: none — these four resource-allocation items are the only ones that qualified at the configured thresholds. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, CONC001]
